name: Boron trifluoride

bonding.summary: Boron bonded to three fluorines in a flat triangle, with an empty orbital.
bonding.electronSharing: Boron shares its three electrons with three fluorines, leaving only six electrons around it. Its empty p orbital eagerly accepts a lone pair from other molecules (a Lewis acid).

formation: B2O3 + 3 CaF2 + 3 H2SO4 -> 2 BF3 + 3 CaSO4 + 3 H2O
uses: Catalyst in organic chemistry and polymerization
facts: BF3 is the textbook example of a molecule with an incomplete octet.
summary: BF3 is electron-poor boron's classic molecule, hungry for a lone pair.

name: Beryllium chloride (gas-phase monomer)

bonding.summary: In the gas, a straight Cl–Be–Cl molecule; in the solid, chains of bridged BeCl4 tetrahedra.
bonding.electronSharing: Beryllium shares its two electrons with two chlorines, ending with just four electrons around it, so it pulls in extra chlorine lone pairs when it can.

facts: BeCl2 is a standard example of a linear molecule in VSEPR theory.
hazards: Toxic; beryllium compounds cause lung disease.
summary: Gas-phase BeCl2 is a perfectly linear molecule with an electron-poor center.

name: Diborane

structure.note: B–H terminal 119 pm, B–H bridging 133 pm.

bonding.summary: Four normal B–H bonds plus two 'banana' bridges where one H holds both borons.
bonding.electronSharing: Boron lacks electrons, so each bridging hydrogen shares a single pair between two borons: a three-centre two-electron bond. Thin lines show the two halves of each bridge.
bonding.geometry: Two BH2 groups linked by two bridging H
bonding.bondLengths: B–H(terminal) 119 pm, B–H(bridge) 133 pm, B···B 177 pm

uses: Making boron compounds and reducing agents
facts: Explaining diborane's bridges helped William Lipscomb win the 1976 Nobel Prize.
summary: Diborane's bridging hydrogens showed chemists that a bond can link three atoms.

name: Silane

bonding.summary: Silicon's analogue of methane.
bonding.electronSharing: Silicon shares one pair with each of four hydrogens. Hydrogen is slightly more electronegative (2.20 vs 1.90), so the electrons lean toward H, the reverse of methane.

uses: Depositing silicon films in chips and solar cells
facts: Silane ignites spontaneously in air.
summary: Silane is silicon's version of methane and a source of pure silicon films.

name: Silicon tetrachloride

bonding.summary: Silicon tetrahedrally bonded to four chlorines.
bonding.electronSharing: Silicon shares a pair with each chlorine; chlorine pulls them toward itself (Δχ 1.26).

facts: It fumes in moist air, reacting with water to form silica and HCl.
summary: SiCl4 is a route to the purest silicon and glass for optical fiber.

name: Germane

bonding.summary: Germanium tetrahedrally bonded to four hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: Germanium shares one pair with each H; the polarity is small (Δχ 0.19).

facts: Germane was detected in the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn.
summary: Germane is germanium's methane, used to grow semiconductor films.

name: Arsine

bonding.summary: A pyramid like ammonia, but much flatter at the top.
bonding.electronSharing: Arsenic shares one pair with each H and keeps a lone pair in an s-rich orbital, so the H–As–H angle is only 92°.

facts: The Marsh test for arsenic poisoning (1836) turned arsenic into arsine and caught it as a mirror on glass.
summary: Arsine is a deadly gas vital to the semiconductor industry.

name: Hydrogen selenide

bonding.summary: A bent molecule like H2S with an even smaller angle.
bonding.electronSharing: Selenium shares one pair with each H and keeps two lone pairs; Δχ is 0.35.

uses: Making selenium semiconductors and solar cells
facts: It is more acidic than H2S because the H–Se bond is weaker.
summary: H2Se is the selenium cousin of water and hydrogen sulfide.

name: Phosphine

bonding.summary: A pyramid with a lone pair on phosphorus.
bonding.electronSharing: Phosphorus and hydrogen have almost the same electronegativity (2.19 vs 2.20), so the pairs are shared evenly.

occurrence: Found in Jupiter and Saturn; traces from anaerobic decay.
facts: A 2020 claim of phosphine in Venus's clouds sparked debate about possible life there.
summary: Phosphine is a toxic gas and a debated biosignature on Venus.

name: Phosphorus trichloride

bonding.summary: Phosphorus bonded to three chlorines with a lone pair on top.
bonding.electronSharing: Phosphorus shares one pair with each chlorine (Δχ 0.97) and keeps one lone pair.

uses: Making herbicides (glyphosate), insecticides and flame retardants
facts: It is one of the most important phosphorus intermediates, made in over a million tonnes a year.
summary: PCl3 is the gateway to most organophosphorus chemicals.

name: Phosphorus pentachloride

bonding.summary: Five P–Cl bonds: three around the middle and two longer ones at the poles.
bonding.electronSharing: Phosphorus uses all five valence electrons to bond to five chlorines, going beyond an octet; the axial bonds are longer and weaker.

facts: In the solid it rearranges into ions: [PCl4]+ [PCl6]−.
summary: PCl5 is the classic trigonal bipyramidal molecule.

name: Phosphorus pentoxide

bonding.summary: A P4O6 cage with one extra oxygen sticking out from each phosphorus.
bonding.electronSharing: Each phosphorus shares pairs with three bridging oxygens and makes a short P=O bond to a terminal oxygen.

facts: It grabs water so strongly it can pull H2O out of sulfuric and nitric acids.
summary: P4O10 is a cage molecule and one of the strongest drying agents known.

name: Sulfur hexafluoride

bonding.summary: Six fluorines around sulfur at the corners of an octahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur's six valence electrons each pair with a fluorine electron; the fluorines pull strongly, but the symmetric shape makes SF6 nonpolar and extremely inert.

facts: It is about 23,500 times stronger than CO2 as a greenhouse gas over 100 years.
Breathing it makes your voice sound very deep.
hazards: Non-toxic but a potent greenhouse gas.
summary: SF6 is an extremely stable insulating gas and a powerful greenhouse gas.

name: Chlorine trifluoride

bonding.summary: A T-shaped molecule: three fluorines and two lone pairs around chlorine.
bonding.electronSharing: Chlorine shares three of its seven electrons with fluorines and keeps two lone pairs, which take the equatorial positions and bend the long axial bonds slightly.

facts: It sets fire to sand, asbestos and glass, and it famously burned through a concrete floor in a 1950s spill.
summary: ClF3 is one of the most aggressive fluorinating agents known.

name: Bromine pentafluoride

bonding.summary: Five fluorines form a square pyramid; a lone pair sits under the base.
bonding.electronSharing: Bromine shares five electrons with fluorines and keeps one lone pair, which pushes the four base fluorines slightly up.

facts: Geologists use BrF5 to release oxygen from minerals to measure isotopes.
summary: BrF5 shows the square-pyramidal shape predicted by VSEPR.

name: Iodine heptafluoride

bonding.summary: Seven fluorines around iodine: two at the poles, five in a ring.
bonding.electronSharing: Iodine uses all seven valence electrons to bond to seven fluorines, the largest number of bonds of any simple main-group molecule.

facts: It is the only common example of a pentagonal bipyramidal molecule.
summary: IF7 packs seven atoms around iodine in a rare pentagonal bipyramid.

name: Titanium tetrachloride

bonding.summary: A tetrahedral molecule; unusually for a metal compound, it is a liquid.
bonding.electronSharing: Titanium shares its four valence electrons with four chlorines and has no d electrons left, so TiCl4 is colorless.

facts: It reacts with moist air to make thick white smoke, used for skywriting and smoke screens.
summary: TiCl4 is a volatile liquid on the route to titanium metal and white pigment.

name: Aluminium chloride (Al2Cl6 dimer)

bonding.summary: Two AlCl4 tetrahedra sharing an edge through two bridging chlorines.
bonding.electronSharing: Each aluminium has only six electrons in AlCl3, so a chlorine on one molecule donates a lone pair to the aluminium of the other, giving both an octet.

facts: It sublimes at 180 °C into Al2Cl6 dimers.
summary: AlCl3 pairs up into Al2Cl6 so each aluminium can complete its octet.

name: Osmium tetroxide

bonding.summary: Osmium in its +8 state with four double-bonded oxygens.
bonding.electronSharing: Osmium has given all eight valence electrons to bonds with four oxygens.

occurrence: Forms slowly when osmium powder is exposed to air.
uses: Catalyst for making diols from alkenes
facts: It is one of very few compounds with an element in the +8 oxidation state.
summary: OsO4 shows osmium in its highest oxidation state, +8.

name: Ruthenium tetroxide

bonding.summary: Ruthenium in its +8 state with four oxygens.
bonding.electronSharing: Ruthenium shares all eight valence electrons with four oxygens.

facts: It can decompose explosively above about 100 °C.
summary: RuO4 is the volatile, aggressive cousin of osmium tetroxide.

name: Xenon difluoride

bonding.summary: A linear F–Xe–F molecule; xenon keeps three lone pairs.
bonding.electronSharing: Xenon shares one electron pair across both Xe–F bonds (a three-centre four-electron bond). Its three lone pairs sit around its waist, so the molecule is straight.

facts: It can be made simply by exposing xenon and fluorine to sunlight.
summary: XeF2 proves that noble gases can form stable compounds.

name: Xenon tetrafluoride

bonding.summary: Four fluorines in a square around xenon; two lone pairs above and below.
bonding.electronSharing: Xenon shares four of its eight electrons with fluorines and keeps two lone pairs, which sit opposite each other.

facts: XeF4 was made in 1962, weeks after Bartlett's first xenon compound.
summary: XeF4 is a square-planar molecule, a textbook VSEPR example.

name: Krypton difluoride

bonding.summary: A linear molecule like XeF2, but much less stable.
bonding.electronSharing: Krypton's electrons are held more tightly than xenon's, so only fluorine can pull them into bonds, and weakly.

formation: Kr + F2 -> KrF2 (electric discharge or UV at about −196 °C)
uses: The strongest known oxidizing and fluorinating agent in research
facts: KrF2 can oxidize gold to the +5 state; it decomposes slowly at room temperature.
summary: KrF2 is the main compound of krypton and a ferocious oxidizer.

name: Argon fluorohydride

bonding.summary: H–Ar covalent, Ar–F largely ionic: roughly (HAr)+ F−.
bonding.electronSharing: Argon shares a pair with hydrogen while fluorine takes most of an electron, forming an ion pair that only survives in frozen argon.

formation: HF photolysed in solid argon below −246 °C
occurrence: Made in 2000 at the University of Helsinki.
facts: It is the only known neutral argon compound and falls apart above about −246 °C.
summary: HArF showed that even argon can form a chemical bond.

name: Hassium tetroxide

bonding.summary: Predicted to be a tetrahedral molecule like OsO4.
bonding.electronSharing: Hassium, like osmium, appears to share all eight valence electrons with four oxygens.

formation: Hs + 2 O2 -> HsO4 (single atoms in a gas stream)
occurrence: Made one molecule at a time at GSI, Germany, in 2001.
uses: Testing the periodic table at its heaviest end
facts: Only seven HsO4 molecules were detected in the first experiment.
summary: HsO4 showed that element 108 behaves like osmium, as the periodic table predicts.

name: Chromium hexacarbonyl

bonding.summary: Six CO ligands around a chromium atom in its zero oxidation state.
bonding.electronSharing: Each CO donates its carbon lone pair to chromium, while chromium pushes d electrons back into CO's empty orbitals (back-bonding). Chromium ends up with 18 valence electrons.

uses: Catalysts and reagents in organic chemistry
facts: It obeys the 18-electron rule, like a transition-metal octet.
summary: Cr(CO)6 is a textbook example of metal–carbonyl bonding.

name: Iron pentacarbonyl

bonding.summary: Five CO ligands around iron(0) in a trigonal bipyramid.
bonding.electronSharing: Each CO donates a lone pair to iron; iron back-donates d electrons to CO. Iron reaches 18 valence electrons.

facts: It is a straw-colored liquid metal compound at room temperature.
summary: Fe(CO)5 is a liquid iron compound used to make ultrapure iron powder.

name: Nickel tetracarbonyl

bonding.summary: Four CO ligands around nickel(0) in a tetrahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Each CO donates a carbon lone pair to nickel, which back-donates d electrons; nickel ends with 18 electrons.

formation: Ni + 4 CO -> Ni(CO)4 (50 °C); reversed at 230 °C to deposit pure nickel (Mond process)
facts: Discovered in 1890, it was the first metal carbonyl known.
summary: Ni(CO)4 lets nickel be carried away as a gas and redeposited in pure form.

name: Ferrocene

bonding.summary: An iron atom sandwiched between two flat, aromatic five-carbon rings.
bonding.electronSharing: Each C5H5− ring has six π electrons spread over all five carbons. Iron(II) bonds to the whole ring at once rather than to individual carbons, reaching 18 electrons.

uses: Building block for catalysts and materials
facts: Its 1951 discovery launched modern organometallic chemistry; the 1973 Nobel Prize honored work on its sandwich structure.
summary: Ferrocene's sandwich structure opened a new field of chemistry.

name: Cisplatin

bonding.summary: Platinum(II) at the center of a square with two Cl and two NH3 on the same side.
bonding.electronSharing: Each NH3 donates its nitrogen lone pair to platinum; the chlorides bond more ionically. In cells, the chlorides are replaced by DNA bases.

uses: Chemotherapy for testicular, ovarian, lung and other cancers
facts: Discovered as an anticancer drug by accident in 1965, when platinum electrodes stopped bacteria from dividing.
The trans isomer is not an effective drug.
summary: Cisplatin binds DNA in cancer cells and has cured most cases of testicular cancer.

name: Chloroauric acid (tetrachloroaurate ion)

bonding.summary: Gold(III) surrounded by four chlorides in a square.
bonding.electronSharing: Gold(III) has eight d electrons and, like platinum(II), prefers four bonds in a flat square.

formation: Au + HNO3 + 4 HCl -> HAuCl4 + NO + 2 H2O (aqua regia)
occurrence: Made by dissolving gold in aqua regia.
facts: Reducing it gently makes gold nanoparticles that look ruby red, as in medieval stained glass.
summary: Chloroauric acid is what gold becomes when it dissolves in aqua regia.

name: Tetraamminecopper(II) ion

bonding.summary: Four ammonia molecules donate lone pairs to a Cu2+ ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each NH3 nitrogen gives its lone pair to empty copper orbitals, forming coordinate bonds; this changes how copper's d electrons absorb light, giving deep blue-violet.
bonding.geometry: Square planar (two water molecules bind weakly above and below)

occurrence: Forms when ammonia is added to copper salt solutions.
facts: Adding ammonia turns pale blue copper sulfate solution an intense deep blue.
summary: The deep blue copper–ammonia complex is a classic demonstration of coordinate bonding.

name: Tetraethyllead

bonding.summary: Lead bonded tetrahedrally to four ethyl groups.
bonding.electronSharing: Lead shares one pair with each ethyl carbon. The weak Pb–C bonds break easily in hot engines, releasing radicals that stop knocking.

occurrence: Synthetic; banned from road fuel worldwide by 2021. It decomposes near 200 °C before boiling.
uses: Still used in some aviation gasoline
facts: The same chemist, Thomas Midgley, introduced both leaded petrol and CFCs.
summary: Tetraethyllead made petrol engines run smoothly but spread lead pollution worldwide.
